miniLesson.modelText:
A community centre should not replace all its in-person classes with online sessions. Online provision can reduce travel and help people whose schedules make attendance difficult. However, a complete replacement would exclude residents who lack reliable internet access or a quiet place to study. A mixed approach would preserve access while offering more flexibility.
The strongest case for online classes is convenience. A parent who cannot travel in the evening may still be able to attend from home. Recorded demonstrations can also help learners review a difficult skill. These benefits are important, but they depend on suitable devices, accessible materials, and support when technology fails.
In-person classes offer a different kind of value. Learners can share equipment, receive immediate practical guidance, and build local relationships. These advantages are especially relevant to courses that involve tools or collaborative work. They cannot always be reproduced by a video call.
The centre should therefore offer online options where they suit the learning activity, rather than treating one format as universally superior. Before changing the programme, staff could ask current learners about their access needs and run a small pilot. Attendance, completion, and learner feedback would provide a stronger basis for a decision than assumptions about what all residents prefer.

Dear Admissions Committee, I am applying for the postgraduate programme in public policy because I want to develop the analytical skills needed to evaluate local services. My interest grew from volunteering at a community centre, where I helped collect feedback about evening activities. That experience showed me how a practical decision can affect people with different needs.
My main responsibility was to organize comments from participants into a short summary for the coordinator. I grouped recurring concerns, checked unclear responses, and separated direct observations from my own interpretations. The work was modest, but it taught me the importance of accurate reporting. It also exposed a limitation: I could describe patterns, yet I lacked the statistical knowledge to assess how representative those patterns were.
A programme that combines policy analysis with research methods would help me address that gap. Before submitting this letter, I would verify the relevant modules and explain how their assessed work relates to my goals. I am particularly interested in learning to compare options, communicate uncertainty, and evaluate results rather than merely propose changes.
After graduation, I hope to work with organizations that improve access to local services. I would bring careful listening, practical experience, and a willingness to revise my assumptions. Thank you for considering my application. Yours sincerely, Alex Chen

miniLesson.modelText:
A proposal to expand a community programme should be judged neither by enthusiasm alone nor by a single disappointing result. The relevant question is whether the available evidence supports a particular expansion under identifiable conditions. That distinction matters because both advocates and critics can describe the same pilot accurately while drawing conclusions that extend beyond what it shows.
Suppose a short evening programme attracted steady attendance but required more staff time than expected. Supporters might emphasize demand, while critics focus on cost. Neither observation is necessarily wrong. Yet attendance does not establish long-term value, and an initial staffing difficulty does not prove that a revised arrangement would fail. A useful assessment separates these findings and asks what additional information would make the decision more reliable.
The first step is to clarify the proposed benefit. If the aim is access, participation by residents who could not attend daytime sessions is more relevant than total attendance alone. If the aim is learning, evidence of attendance must be distinguished from evidence of progress. The measure should follow the purpose rather than be selected afterwards because it makes the programme look successful.
The second step is to identify constraints without treating them as fixed by default. Staff time, room availability, and support needs may limit expansion, but some limits could be addressed through a narrower schedule or a different format. Those alternatives should be compared on the same basis, with their costs and uncertainties made explicit.
A proportionate recommendation would therefore preserve the most promising elements while requiring a better-defined evaluation. It might support a limited extension, specify the information to collect, and name a date for review. Such a conclusion is less dramatic than declaring the programme an unquestionable success or failure. It is also more useful, because it tells decision-makers what to do next and what would justify changing course.
This approach does not eliminate disagreement. It gives disagreement a clearer object: the purpose, evidence, assumptions, and trade-offs behind the proposed action. That clarity is the main contribution of a careful synthesis.

title: Audience and controlled register

miniLesson.markdown:
Adapt emphasis, structure, and terminology for the reader while keeping facts and important limitations stable. Precision comes from clear relationships, not unnecessary complexity.

Lesson focus: Explain for a non-specialist. Read the model, notice the target choice, then practise it before writing your own version. Use truthful details; do not copy the model as your own experience.
miniLesson.modelText:
The same proposal may need to be explained to a technical reviewer, a community participant, and a funding committee. Effective adaptation changes the route into the argument, not the underlying facts. If a writer simplifies by removing every limitation, the result is not accessible communication but a different and less defensible claim.
For a technical reviewer, the account might begin with the evaluation question, method, and limits of the data. The reader needs enough detail to assess whether the reasoning is sound. Terms should be defined where ambiguity could affect interpretation, and uncertainty should be connected to its source rather than expressed through vague caution.
For community participants, the opening might instead explain the practical change and why their experience matters. Shorter sentences and familiar examples can reduce unnecessary effort. However, the explanation should still distinguish what has been observed from what is being proposed. Participants deserve to know whether a decision is provisional, what alternatives were considered, and how they can respond.
A funding committee may need a third structure: the need, proposed action, evidence of feasibility, expected benefit, and evaluation plan. A concise account can make these relationships visible without suggesting that funding will guarantee the desired outcome. Specific commitments are more credible than sweeping promises, especially when the proposal depends on cooperation from other organizations.
Across these versions, the writer should preserve stable facts and accurate attribution. Numbers, roles, and observed outcomes must not change to suit the audience. The amount of methodological detail may vary, but a material limitation cannot simply disappear. If the same term has different meanings for different readers, the writer should explain the intended meaning rather than rely on apparent familiarity.
Controlled register is therefore a form of judgment. Formal language is not automatically more precise, and simple language is not automatically less rigorous. The appropriate version is the one that enables its reader to understand the decision, assess the relevant evidence, and act without being misled.

Practical experience has given me a useful starting point, but it has also made me cautious about presenting competence as certainty. My aim is to develop methods that allow a decision to be both workable and open to revision.
In a small volunteer project, I helped prepare a briefing from participants' comments. I organized the material, documented unresolved questions, and checked whether the summary represented disagreement fairly. The resulting account informed planning, although it did not establish the wider community's preferences. This distinction is important to my application: the experience demonstrates careful communication and awareness of evidence limits, not independent mastery of policy research.
My next step is therefore methodological. I want to understand how research design, analysis, and institutional context shape the conclusions a project can support. In an actual application, I would connect this aim to verified elements of the current programme and explain why their assessed work addresses my specific needs. I would distinguish compulsory provision from optional opportunities and avoid presenting a promotional description as evidence of a guaranteed experience.
I would contribute a habit of documenting decisions, willingness to examine competing interpretations, and practical familiarity with collaborative work. These qualities are not unique, but they are relevant. They would help me participate responsibly while learning from classmates whose experience challenges my own assumptions. I also recognize that further study may refine or change my initial professional direction.
Before submission, I would revise this letter against three questions. Does each claim have appropriate support? Does each paragraph perform a distinct function? Does the level of certainty match what I can actually know? I would then check factual details and remove wording that merely amplifies praise without adding information.
My longer-term intention is to help organizations communicate the basis and limits of their decisions. I do not regard admission as proof that this aim will be achieved. I regard study as an opportunity to test my preparation, deepen it, and make its limitations more explicit. Thank you for considering my application. Yours sincerely, Alex Chen

Invent a dramatic result for attention.
warmups.answer: Explain the action and why it matters.

options: Remove praise that adds no information.
Remove every factual limitation.
warmups.answer: Remove praise that adds no information.

task.title: Control rhetorical emphasis
task.prompt: Revise a formal application so its strongest evidence receives emphasis without overstating achievements or disparaging other applicants.
